stages.note: Your cluster gets a virtual node. Pods you send there run on the GPU in AWS. From here on, run the commands below, or ask your AI to run them one at a time.

steps.d: Your cluster administrator gives you a kubeconfig file. The node list must show the nodes of the cluster that gets the GPU. The last command must print yes: the connector install needs cluster-admin rights.
steps.c:
export KUBECONFIG=/path/to/kubeconfig
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get nodes
kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces

steps.d: The Server Version must be 1.30 or later. The second command must print one line.
steps.c:
kubectl version
kubectl api-resources | grep validatingadmissionpolicies

steps.h: Find your pod and service CIDRs
steps.d: Write down both values. You need them when you install the connector.
steps.c:
# any cluster: Kubernetes 1.33 or later
kubectl get servicecidrs -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CIDRS:.spec.cidrs
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NODE:.metadata.name,PODCIDRS:.spec.podCIDRs
# kubeadm clusters: the whole pod range
kubectl -n kube-system get cm kubeadm-config \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.ClusterConfiguration}' | grep -E 'podSubnet|serviceSubnet'
steps.g: k3s: the defaults are 10.42.0.0/16 (pods) and 10.43.0.0/16 (services), unless your k3s server uses --cluster-cidr or --service-cidr. The node podCIDRs are slices of the pod range: with several nodes, ask your cluster administrator for the whole range. Other clusters: ask your cluster administrator.

steps.h: Check that the API server reaches pods
steps.d: It must print ok (or OK). A 502 means the API server cannot reach pod addresses (OrbStack Kubernetes does this): kubectl logs, exec and port-forward to the pool then fail. Use another cluster, for example kind or k3s.
steps.c:
P=$(kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl get --raw "/api/v1/namespaces/kube-system/pods/$P:8080/proxy/health"

steps.d: The output names your network plugin, for example calico, cilium or flannel. Tell your Multicloud contact.
steps.c: kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o name | grep -E 'cilium|calico|flannel|weave|antrea|canal'

steps.d: The virtual node needs about 115m of free CPU requests on one of your nodes. If every node shows 95% or more CPU requested, add capacity first.
steps.c: kubectl describe nodes | grep -A8 'Allocated resources'

steps.d: Good result: docker hub 401, ghcr 401, cloudflare 200. A connection or certificate error means your network blocks the connector. No inbound port is needed. If you use an HTTPS proxy or TLS inspection, tell your Multicloud contact.
in: Egress path: direct, proxy or TLS inspection

stages.note: A pool is the capacity in your AWS account that Multicloud manages for you. The pool keeps one worker running while it is awake, and you pay AWS for that worker. Create the pool only when your GPU quota is 4 or more.

steps.h: Create the pool with GPU settings
steps.d: Replace <cloud-account-id> with your cloud-account ID. The settings allow L4 or A10G only, on-demand only (no interruptions), and a 100 GB disk for the model. A cap of $1.50 per hour allows both GPU types.
steps.c:
cat > poc-gpu.json <<'EOF'
{"settings": {"regions": ["us-east-1"], "accelerator_names": ["L4", "A10G"],
              "max_risk": 0, "min_storage_gb": 100,
              "max_memory_gb": 16}}
EOF
mctl extend create poc-gpu --cloud-account <cloud-account-id> --max-servers 2 \
  --max-cost-per-hour 1.5 --from-file poc-gpu.json

steps.h: Wait until the pool is ready
steps.d: Run the command every minute. Status: ready means the pool is ready. Status: provisioning (…) means it is still starting; the first start takes several minutes. If the status stays provisioning for more than 20 minutes, send the output to your Multicloud contact.
steps.c: mctl pool show poc-gpu

steps.h: Pause the pool when you stop for the day
steps.d: A hibernated pool runs no worker and costs nothing. Wake it when you continue.
steps.c:
mctl pool hibernate poc-gpu
mctl pool wake poc-gpu --wait

stages.note: A CPU pool for burst work. The pool keeps one worker running while it is awake, and you pay AWS for that worker.

steps.d: Replace <cloud-account-id> and the region. Three servers at most, at most $0.50 per hour together.
steps.c:
cat > burst.json <<'EOF'
{"settings": {"regions": ["us-east-1"]}}
EOF
mctl extend create burst --cloud-account <cloud-account-id> --max-servers 3 \
  --max-cost-per-hour 0.5 --from-file burst.json

steps.h: Wait until the pool is ready
steps.d: Run it every minute. Status: ready means ready. Still provisioning after 20 minutes: send the output to your Multicloud contact.
steps.c: mctl pool show burst

stages.t: Connect your cluster to the pool
stages.note: Your Multicloud contact joins you for this stage. Check first that kubectl points at your own cluster (kubectl config current-context).

steps.d: --gpu 1 lets your cluster use 1 GPU of the pool. Without --gpu, the pool grants no GPU. The output starts with Peering <id> created. Write down the peering ID. Copy the full line after Install command: you need it in the next step. To see both again, run: mctl peering list poc-gpu --json | jq -r '.peerings[] | "\(.id) \(.helm_command)"'
steps.c:
mctl peering create poc-gpu --gpu 1 --cpu-millicores 4000 --memory-mb 14336 \
  --pods 110 --ephemeral-storage-mb 51200

steps.d: The pool default grant. The output starts with Peering <id> created and has an Install command line. Then continue with install-connector.
steps.c: mctl peering create burst

steps.who: You run it, with your CIDRs
steps.d: Paste the helm command from the Install command line. Replace <POD_CIDR> and <SERVICE_CIDR> with the values from “Prepare your cluster”. Do not change the other values. It looks like the example below, with your own IDs.
steps.c:
helm install liqo-consumer oci://registry-1.docker.io/multicloud/liqo-consumer-chart \
  --version 0.3.1 -n liqo --create-namespace \
  --set liqo.ipam.podCIDR=<POD_CIDR> --set liqo.ipam.serviceCIDR=<SERVICE_CIDR> \
  --set liqo.discovery.config.clusterID=c-…  --set-string reflectionKick.remoteClusterID=…

steps.d: Multicloud gives the connection file only once, on the first read after the peering is ready. This loop waits for it and saves it. Replace <peering-id> (and the pool name, if yours is not poc-gpu). The file must not be empty. Keep it secret: it grants access to the pool. Do not run mctl peering show by hand before the loop ends.
steps.c:
POOL=poc-gpu ID=<peering-id>
(
  umask 077
  while true; do
    if mctl peering show "$POOL" "$ID" --json > peering.new; then
      mv peering.new peering.json
      jq -e '.bundle != null' peering.json >/dev/null && break
      status=$(jq -r .status peering.json); echo "Status: $status"
      [ "$status" = PENDING ] || break
    else
      rc=$?; [ "$rc" -eq 3 ] || [ "$rc" -eq 4 ] && { echo "mctl exit $rc: stop"; break; }
    fi
    sleep 10
  done
  rm -f peering.new
  jq -er '.bundle // empty' peering.json > multicloud-peering.yaml && rm peering.json
)
steps.g: If the status is SUSPENDED, wake the pool (mctl pool wake poc-gpu --wait) and run the loop again. If the status is FAILED or the file is empty, revoke the peering (mctl peering revoke poc-gpu <peering-id> --yes) and ask for one GPU again.

steps.d: The check Job name ends with your consumer cluster ID (c- and 8 characters), not the peering ID. Find it in the line Consumer cluster of mctl peering show poc-gpu <peering-id>, or in the clusterID value of your helm command.
steps.c:
kubectl apply -f multicloud-peering.yaml
kubectl -n liqo wait --for=condition=complete --timeout=10m \
  job/multicloud-peering-preflight-<consumer-cluster-id>

steps.h: Check that the GPU shows up
steps.d: The virtual node needs about 2 minutes. The output must be 1. An empty output in the first minutes is normal: run it again.
steps.c:
kubectl get node -l liqo.io/type=virtual-node \
  -o jsonpath='{..allocatable.nvidia\.com/gpu}'

steps.d: The virtual node must be Ready and show the pool slug in the last column. It needs about 2 minutes after the bundle.
steps.c: kubectl get nodes -l liqo.io/type=virtual-node -L multicloud.io/pool

stages.note: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct fits the 24 GB of an L4 or A10G.

steps.d: Only pods in an offloaded namespace can use the pool. Other pods in my-team still run on your own nodes.
steps.c:
kubectl create namespace my-team
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: offloading.liqo.io/v1beta1
kind: NamespaceOffloading
metadata: {name: offloading, namespace: my-team}
spec:
  namespaceMappingStrategy: DefaultName
  podOffloadingStrategy: LocalAndRemote
  clusterSelector:
    nodeSelectorTerms:
    - matchExpressions:
      - {key: liqo.io/type, operator: In, values: [virtual-node]}
EOF

steps.d: vLLM refuses a request without this key. The key stays in your cluster.
steps.c:
kubectl -n my-team create secret generic vllm-api-key \
  --from-literal=key="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"

steps.d: Copy this block into a file named vllm-gpu.yaml in your current folder. On the command line: run cat > vllm-gpu.yaml, paste the block, press Enter, then Ctrl+D.
The first start takes up to about 20 minutes: a new GPU worker, the image and a 15 GB model download. The wait command returns when the model is loaded.
steps.c:
kubectl -n my-team apply -f vllm-gpu.yaml
kubectl -n my-team wait --for=condition=available deploy/vllm --timeout=30m
steps.g: To watch the progress, run kubectl -n my-team get pod -l app=vllm -o wide -w in another terminal. Press Ctrl+C to stop the watch.

steps.d: Open a new terminal (on Windows: a new Ubuntu window), point it at your cluster again (export KUBECONFIG=…), and run the command. Keep this terminal open while you send queries. Send the queries from your first terminal.
steps.c: kubectl -n my-team port-forward deploy/vllm 8000:8000
steps.c_agent:
mkdir -p ~/multicloud-onboarding && chmod 700 ~/multicloud-onboarding
nohup kubectl -n my-team port-forward deploy/vllm 8000:8000 >~/multicloud-onboarding/port-forward.log 2>&1 &
echo $! > ~/multicloud-onboarding/port-forward.pid

steps.d: See “Send a query to the model” below.
steps.c_agent:
KEY=$(kubectl -n my-team get secret vllm-api-key -o jsonpath='{.data.key}' | base64 -d)
curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"qwen","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say hello."}]}' | jq -r '.choices[0].message.content'
unset KEY

stages.note: A small pod on the pool proves the path.

steps.d: Only pods in an offloaded namespace can use the pool.
steps.c:
kubectl create namespace my-team
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: offloading.liqo.io/v1beta1
kind: NamespaceOffloading
metadata: {name: offloading, namespace: my-team}
spec:
  namespaceMappingStrategy: DefaultName
  podOffloadingStrategy: LocalAndRemote
  clusterSelector:
    nodeSelectorTerms:
    - matchExpressions:
      - {key: liqo.io/type, operator: In, values: [virtual-node]}
EOF

steps.d: Replace <slug> with the pool slug from the virtual node check (the multicloud.io/pool value). The NODE column must show the virtual node. A cold pool needs about 5 minutes to add a worker.
steps.c:
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: burst-hello, namespace: my-team}
spec:
  tolerations:
  - {key: multicloud.io/pool, operator: Equal, value: <slug>, effect: NoSchedule}
  nodeSelector: {multicloud.io/pool: <slug>}
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: hello
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh", "-c", "echo hello from the pool; uname -n; sleep 30"]
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 64Mi}
EOF
kubectl -n my-team wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/burst-hello --timeout=15m
kubectl -n my-team get pod burst-hello -o wide
kubectl -n my-team logs burst-hello
kubectl -n my-team delete pod burst-hello

stages.note: A GPU worker costs about $0.80–$1.20 per hour while it runs. To pause instead of delete, use mctl pool hibernate poc-gpu. Delete in this order.

steps.h: Remove the PoC from your cluster and Multicloud
steps.d: Stop the port-forward first (Ctrl+C). Replace <peering-id>. Delete the bundle before the revoke: a revoke first makes the bundle delete hang on Liqo finalizers. Do not delete the liqo namespace before helm uninstall finishes. Deleting the pool cannot be undone.
steps.c:
kubectl -n my-team delete -f vllm-gpu.yaml
kubectl -n my-team delete secret vllm-api-key
kubectl delete namespaceoffloadings.offloading.liqo.io --all -A
kubectl delete -f multicloud-peering.yaml --wait=false
# the bridge is gone now, so Liqo cannot clear its own finalizers: clear them
for t in namespacemaps.offloading.liqo.io resourceslices.authentication.liqo.io; do
  kubectl get $t -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{" "}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}' |
    while read ns n; do kubectl -n "$ns" patch $t "$n" --type=merge -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'; done
done
mctl peering revoke poc-gpu <peering-id> --yes
kubectl delete foreignclusters.core.liqo.io --all
helm uninstall liqo-consumer -n liqo --wait --timeout 10m
kubectl delete namespace liqo my-team
mctl pool delete poc-gpu --yes

steps.d: Wait a few minutes after the pool delete. Both commands must print nothing. If a Multicloud instance still shows after 15 minutes, tell your Multicloud contact. Replace <region> with the pool region (repeat the command for each region of the pool), and run it with the AWS profile of the connection (export AWS_PROFILE=<profile>).
steps.c:
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations,validatingwebhookconfigurations | grep liqo
aws ec2 describe-instances --region <region> \
  --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=pending,running Name=tag-key,Values=multicloud-cluster-id \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType]' --output text

steps.h: Keep or remove the AWS connection
steps.d: To continue after the PoC, keep it. To remove it: disconnect the account, which stops Multicloud and removes what it created in your account. Then remove the IAM role from the folder you made when you connected AWS (the folder with multicloud.tf), with the same AWS profile. Type yes when OpenTofu asks.
steps.c:
mctl cloud-account disconnect <cloud-account-id> --wait
cd <connection-folder>        # the folder with multicloud.tf, for example ~/multicloud-aws
export AWS_PROFILE=<profile> AWS_REGION=<region>
tofu destroy
